title: Physics: An Introduction
lead: Physics is concerned with describing the interactions of energy, matter, space, and time, and a surprisingly small and unified set of physical laws explains what we observe. This section says what the realm of physics is and where physics is applied, what scientists mean by a model, a theory, and a law, and how experiment decides between them. It ends with the conditions under which classical physics is an excellent approximation and with the two theories, relativity and quantum mechanics, that make up modern physics.
objectives: Explain the difference between a principle and a law.
Explain the difference between a model and a theory.
summary_html:
• Science seeks to discover and describe the underlying order and simplicity in nature.
  • Physics is the most basic of the sciences, concerning itself with energy, matter, space and time, and their interactions.
  • Scientific laws and theories express the general truths of nature and the body of knowledge they encompass. These laws of nature are rules that all natural processes appear to follow.

figures.original_caption: What is a model? This planetary model of the atom shows electrons orbiting the nucleus. It is a drawing that we use to form a mental image of the atom that we cannot see directly with our eyes because it is too small.

exercises.prompt: A friend tells you they have learned about a new law of nature. What can you know about the information even before your friend describes the law? How would the information be different if your friend told you they had learned about a scientific theory rather than a law?

answer.solution: Without knowing the details of the law, you can still infer that the information your friend has learned conforms to the requirements of all laws of nature: it will be a concise description of the universe around us; a statement of the underlying rules that all natural processes follow. If the information had been a theory, you would be able to infer that the information will be a large-scale, broadly applicable generalization.

exercises.prompt: Models are particularly useful in relativity and quantum mechanics, where conditions are outside those normally encountered by humans. What is a model?

answer.solution: A model is a representation of something that is often too difficult, or impossible, to display directly. It is justified with experimental proof, but it is accurate only under limited situations, and it is meant to describe certain aspects of a physical system rather than all of them. The planetary model of the atom is the example the text gives: we cannot observe electron orbits, but the mental image of electrons going round a nucleus helps explain the observations we can make, such as the light given off by hot gases. That is why models matter so much in relativity and quantum mechanics, where the phenomena are ones we never experience directly and a picture we can relate to in human terms is the way in to them.

exercises.prompt: How does a model differ from a theory?

answer.solution: A model is a picture of something we cannot see directly, and it is meant only to describe certain aspects of a physical system accurately. A theory is a testable explanation for patterns in nature, supported by scientific evidence and verified multiple times by various groups of researchers, and it should describe all aspects of any system that falls within its domain of applicability. Some theories include a model to help visualize the phenomena, as the kinetic theory of gases pictures a gas as atoms and molecules, whereas others do not; Newton’s theory of gravity needs no mental image, because we can observe the objects directly with our own senses. So a model can be part of a theory, but a theory is judged by whether every one of its testable implications is verified, and a model only by whether it helps within the limited situations it is meant for.

exercises.prompt: If two different theories describe experimental observations equally well, can one be said to be more valid than the other (assuming both use accepted rules of logic)?

answer.solution: In the sense the text gives the word, no. A theory is valid when its experimentally testable implications have been verified and none has been shown false, and if two theories account for every observation equally well, then experiment has not yet told them apart. Scientists may still prefer one of them, for example the one that is simpler or the one that covers a wider domain, but that preference is a matter of convenience and elegance, and the text is plain that a theory is right or wrong by experiment no matter how elegant or convenient it is. The way to decide between the two is to find an implication on which they differ and perform that experiment; until then, both are valid within the observations made so far.

exercises.prompt: What determines the validity of a theory?

answer.solution: Experiment does. A theory is a testable explanation for patterns in nature, and any experimentally testable implication of it should be verified; when an experiment shows an implication of the theory to be false, the theory is either thrown out or modified suitably, for example by limiting its domain of applicability. Verification by various groups of researchers, repeated multiple times, is what earns a theory its standing. Note that a theory can never be known with absolute certainty, since it is impossible to perform every imaginable experiment, so physicists take every theory to be valid until a counterexample is observed.

exercises.prompt: Certain criteria must be satisfied if a measurement or observation is to be believed. Will the criteria necessarily be as strict for an expected result as for an unexpected result?

answer.solution: The standard of evidence is the same in principle, and the text gives the reason: the cornerstone of discovering natural laws is observation, science must describe the universe as it is and not as we imagine it to be, and al-Haytham’s lesson is that senses and predisposition can lead to poor conclusions, so a scientist trusts only objective evidence and is ready to reject existing knowledge. In practice an unexpected result is examined more closely, because a good-quality, verifiable experiment that contradicts a well-established law means the law must be modified or overthrown, and no one takes that step before the experiment has been repeated and validated. An expected result agrees with what has already been verified many times, so it carries less weight on its own. You might conclude that the extra scrutiny is about how much a result would overturn, not about holding an unexpected result to a different rule; the danger the text warns about is the opposite one, that an expected result is believed too easily.

exercises.prompt: Can the validity of a model be limited, or must it be universally valid? How does this compare to the required validity of a theory or a law?

answer.solution: The validity of a model is limited by its nature. The text says that while a model is justified with experimental proof, it is only accurate under limited situations, and that a model is meant only to describe certain aspects of a physical system; the planetary model of the atom is useful for picturing atomic spectra and no one expects it to be the whole truth about an atom. A theory is held to more: it should describe all aspects of any system that falls within its domain of applicability, and a law is a concise and very general statement that is supported by repeated experiments. Both a theory and a law must hold everywhere within their domain, and a single good-quality, verifiable experiment against them means they are modified or overthrown. Note, though, that even a theory or a law has a domain, since classical physics is an excellent approximation only under stated conditions, so the difference is that a model may be knowingly partial, whereas a theory or a law is expected to hold throughout the range it claims.

exercises.prompt: Classical physics is a good approximation to modern physics under certain circumstances. What are they?

answer.solution: Three conditions must be met. Matter must be moving at speeds less than about 1% of the speed of light, the objects dealt with must be large enough to be seen with a microscope, and only weak gravitational fields, such as the field generated by the Earth, can be involved. Because humans live under such circumstances, classical physics seems intuitively reasonable, and it gives an extremely accurate description of the universe under a wide range of everyday circumstances.

exercises.prompt: When is it necessary to use relativistic quantum mechanics?

answer.solution: Relativistic quantum mechanics is the combination of relativity and quantum mechanics, and it is necessary when both are needed at once: for objects smaller than can be seen with a microscope that are traveling at greater than about 1% of the speed of light or experiencing a strong gravitational field such as that near the Sun. It is the best universally applicable theory we have, but because of its mathematical complexity it is used only when necessary, and the other theories are used whenever they will produce sufficiently accurate results.

exercises.prompt: Can classical physics be used to accurately describe a satellite moving at a speed of 7500 m/s? Explain why or why not.

answer.solution: Yes. Check the satellite against the three conditions. The speed of light is about $3 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$, so 7500 m/s is $2.5 \times 10^{-5}$ of it, which is 0.0025%, far below the 1% at which relativity must be used. A satellite is far larger than anything that needs a microscope to be seen, so quantum mechanics is not needed. The gravitational field it moves in is the Earth’s, which the text names as the example of a weak field. All three conditions are met, so classical physics describes the satellite’s motion accurately. Note that the GPS satellites the section mentions do carry small relativistic corrections, but only because they keep time to nanoseconds, which is the effect of time dilation the passage on GPS hints at; the motion itself is classical.
